articles.title: Chemistry textbooks have been getting this wrong for nearly 100 years
articles.summary: A foundational chemistry concept found in textbooks for almost 100 years may have been taught incorrectly. Researchers say the inductive effect in neutral molecules appears to extend only across one chemical bond, rather than gradually weakening over three or four bonds as traditionally taught. The team argues that updating this explanation could make organic chemistry easier to understand and provide a stronger foundation for future research and innovation.
articles.content:
A chemistry concept taught to generations of students may need to be explained very differently, according to an international team of researchers who say a long-accepted textbook description does not match modern evidence.

The issue centers on the inductive effect, a fundamental idea in structural organic chemistry used to describe how atoms influence the distribution of electrons within molecules. The researchers' 2024 research concluded that textbooks had been describing this effect incorrectly for almost 100 years.

That work has already begun to influence chemistry education. Two A-level exam boards have since announced reviews of how they teach the inductive effect and directly cited the research as part of the reason for doing so.

A new paper in the Journal of Chemical Education now expands on those findings and examines what they could mean for the way one of chemistry's foundational concepts is taught.

Rethinking a Core Idea in Organic Chemistry

Researchers led by Cardiff University and the University of Newcastle in Australia are proposing a simpler and more consistent explanation of the inductive effect. They believe the revised approach could make the concept easier for students to understand while giving scientists a clearer framework for interpreting how molecules behave.

"The inductive effect is a foundational concept in chemical bonding, because it is used to explain how electrons are distributed between atoms in molecules," explains Dr. Mark Elliott, lead author of the study from Cardiff University's School of Chemistry.

"Everyone who studies chemistry beyond GCSE, or equivalent, learns about it."

The implications are particularly important for organic chemistry, according to the researchers. Organic chemists routinely study chains of atoms that form the molecular foundations of medicines, advanced materials, agrochemicals, polymers and many other technologies used in everyday life.

Understanding how electrons are distributed through those structures can help chemists explain why molecules have particular properties and why they undergo certain chemical reactions.

A Chemical Effect That May Stop After One Bond

For decades, organic chemistry textbooks have generally taught that the influence of certain atoms can travel through three or four bonds within a molecule. According to the traditional explanation, that influence becomes progressively weaker as it moves farther from the original atom.

The researchers say the evidence paints a different picture.

"In our latest paper, we find that the inductive effect does not behave in this way," Dr. Elliott says.

"Instead, we show that the inductive effect in a neutral molecule does not extend beyond one bond. As a result of this, we need to refine explanations for certain types of reactivity. This can provide a more coherent framework for explaining chemical structure and reactivity."

Rather than treating the inductive effect as an influence that gradually travels along a chain of atoms, the team's interpretation confines it to the bond directly connected to the relevant atom in a neutral molecule.

That seemingly small change could matter because the inductive effect is commonly used to explain molecular structure and chemical reactions. If its reach has been misunderstood, other explanations built around the traditional model may also need to be reconsidered.

Evidence Hidden Across the Scientific Literature

The researchers did not arrive at the conclusion from a single experiment. They brought together evidence that was already scattered throughout scientific research and combined it with their own consistent data set.

"While some data supporting our conclusions is already available within the research literature, it is not widely known. What we have done is pull all the existing data together, supported by our own coherent data set, to show the generality and teaching implications of this approach.

"It is important to teach the basics correctly. So, if we get rid of this incorrect stuff, we can start using the correct explanation for all aspects."

The international collaboration grew after Dr. Elliott encountered work by Dr. Edwin Johnson of the University of Newcastle and Dr. Kasimir Gregory of the University of New England. Their research examined how electronegative elements affect acidity and also produced results that did not fit conventional textbook descriptions.

"We realized that the discrepancy between modern computational data and textbooks was larger than we had anticipated."

Modern Tools Challenge Longstanding Chemistry Ideas

Questioning such an established concept was not something the researchers initially approached lightly.

"We didn't initially feel comfortable challenging the established wisdom. Some of the names associated with the inductive effect are 'legends' of our discipline. We certainly aren't smarter than those pioneers, of course. But we have better tools nowadays and so have been able to look at things in a different way - examining molecular structures directly whereas they had to draw indirect conclusions from limited experimental data."

Earlier generations of chemists developed many foundational ideas using the experimental techniques available at the time. Modern computational methods now allow researchers to examine molecular structures and electron distributions in ways that were not possible when many textbook explanations were first developed.

By clarifying what the inductive effect does and how far it extends, the researchers hope other influences on molecular behavior can also be understood more accurately.

Why Correcting Chemistry Textbooks Matters

The researchers argue that getting foundational concepts right is important far beyond introductory chemistry courses. Misunderstandings introduced early in a student's education can follow them into more advanced chemistry and eventually into scientific research.

"If a foundational concept is taught inaccurately, misunderstandings can carry into more advanced science and research," adds Dr. Edwin Johnson, Lecturer at the University of Newcastle, Australia, who co-authored the paper.

"By revisiting a long-standing textbook explanation with modern tools, our work aims to improve chemistry education and strengthen the conceptual foundations that support chemical innovation."

The researchers hope their proposed explanation will ultimately give students a more consistent way to understand chemical bonding while providing scientists with a stronger conceptual basis for studying molecular structure and reactivity.

The paper, 'Rethinking the Nature and Extent of Inductive Effects in Organic Compounds', is published in the Journal of Chemical Education.

This correction has already influenced educational boards to review teaching methods, promising clearer understanding for students and stronger foundations for future scientific research and innovation. The impact is broad, affecting chemistry education and research globally, with detailed context and implications provided.
articles.personality_title: Scientists update a key chemistry concept taught for nearly 100 years

articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques révisent un concept clé de chimie enseigné depuis près de 100 ans
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis presque 100 ans, les manuels de chimie expliquent l'effet inductif comme une influence qui se propage progressivement sur trois ou quatre liaisons chimiques dans les molécules. Ce concept aide les élèves à comprendre comment les atomes influencent la répartition des électrons, ce qui est important en chimie organique.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'Université de Cardiff et de l'Université de Newcastle en Australie ont découvert que cette explication traditionnelle n'est pas exacte. Leur étude de 2024 montre que dans les molécules neutres, l'effet inductif ne s'étend qu'à une seule liaison chimique, et non plusieurs. Ils ont rassemblé des preuves issues de nombreuses études scientifiques ainsi que leurs propres données pour soutenir cette nouvelle compréhension.

**Impact** – Ce changement est important car l'effet inductif sert à expliquer le comportement des molécules, notamment leurs réactions et propriétés. Si l'effet ne concerne qu'une liaison, de nombreuses explications dans les manuels et idées scientifiques doivent être mises à jour. Certaines commissions d'examen ont déjà commencé à revoir la manière d'enseigner ce concept. Cette nouvelle explication peut faciliter l'apprentissage et aider les scientifiques à mieux étudier les molécules.

**Prochaine étape** – Les enseignants et auteurs de manuels vont probablement actualiser leurs supports pour refléter cette découverte. Les chercheurs espèrent que cette vision plus claire de l'effet inductif améliorera l'enseignement de la chimie et soutiendra de futures découvertes scientifiques.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle recherche montre que l'effet inductif ne se propage que sur une liaison dans les molécules, modifiant une idée chimique enseignée depuis près d'un siècle et améliorant notre compréhension du comportement moléculaire.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos actualizan un concepto clave de química enseñado durante casi 100 años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante casi 100 años, los libros de química han explicado el efecto inductivo como una influencia que se extiende gradualmente a través de tres o cuatro enlaces químicos en las moléculas. Este concepto ayuda a los estudiantes a entender cómo los átomos afectan la distribución de electrones, lo cual es importante en la química orgánica.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Cardiff y la Universidad de Newcastle en Australia descubrieron que esta explicación tradicional no es correcta. Su estudio de 2024 mostró que en moléculas neutras, el efecto inductivo solo se extiende a través de un enlace químico, no varios. Reunieron pruebas de muchos estudios científicos y sus propios datos para apoyar esta nueva idea.

**Impacto** – Este cambio es importante porque el efecto inductivo se usa para explicar cómo se comportan las moléculas, incluyendo sus reacciones y propiedades. Si el efecto solo llega a un enlace, muchas explicaciones de libros y ideas científicas deben actualizarse. Algunos consejos de examen ya comenzaron a revisar cómo enseñan este concepto. Esta nueva explicación puede facilitar el aprendizaje y ayudar a los científicos a estudiar las moléculas con mayor claridad.

**Próximo paso** – Los profesores y autores de libros probablemente actualizarán sus materiales para reflejar este hallazgo. Los investigadores esperan que esta visión más clara del efecto inductivo mejore la educación en química y apoye mejores descubrimientos científicos.

**Resumen en una frase** – Una nueva investigación muestra que el efecto inductivo en las moléculas solo se extiende a través de un enlace, cambiando una idea de química enseñada por casi un siglo y mejorando cómo entendemos el comportamiento molecular.

articles.title: Donor-funded science is rising in Brazil ― upending a long tradition
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02829-2Philanthropists are stepping up support for research in a country where scientists have relied on the government alone for funding.
articles.content:
Biologist Guilherme Longo, who studies the effect of climate change on coral bleaching, is one of the recipients of funding from Brazilian science philanthropy Serrapilheira.Credit: Erika Beux

Wealthy philanthropies in Brazil are starting to put their money into science — a trend that could help to protect research funding if voters in next month’s elections choose a president who doesn’t prioritize the sciences.

Brazil does not have a strong history of charitable support for research. But the past decade has seen the founding of the nation’s first non-profit organization dedicated to funding scientific research: the Serrapilheira Institute. The organization has now distributed more than US$25 million to early-career researchers, and other philanthropic science funders have sprung up in its wake. Moreover, in 2023, Brazil’s leading university, the University of São Paulo, launched a research centre to study and foster science philanthropy.

This movement is building against a backdrop of turbulent times for Brazilian science. Former president Jair Bolsonaro slashed science funding during his tenure from 2019–23. Polls ahead of Brazil’s presidential election on 4 October show that Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro, is running neck and neck with Brazil’s current president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

This growth chamber, which biologist Paulo Teixeira uses to study plant immunity, was connected to the power grid with money provided by private funder Serrapilheira.Credit: Paulo Teixeira/ESALQ, University of São Paulo

In the United States, “philanthropy has been able to provide a little bit of bridge support” to science, says Kate Lowry, strategy director at the Science Philanthropy Alliance, a New York City-based coalition of heavyweight funders that includes the Gates Foundation in Seattle, Washington, and Wellcome in London. “The same could be true in Brazil.”

Scientists in Brazil who have received philanthropic funding say that it provides a welcome degree of flexibility. For example, biologist Paulo Teixeira, at the Luiz de Queiroz College of Agriculture in Piracicaba, received public funding to build a growth chamber to study the immune system of plants, but his initial proposal didn’t explicitly include the cost of connecting the new building to the electrical grid. So, he used funding from the Serrapilheira Institute to buy a utility pole and make that connection, salvaging his project. “I don’t know what I would’ve done without that money,” he says.

Overcoming hurdles

Historically, scientists at leading public universities in Brazil have been critical of researchers who accept private donations, arguing that science should be fully funded by the government. Big donors, for their part, don’t usually have science on their radar, says philanthropist José Luiz Egydio Setúbal, the head of a foundation focused on child and adolescent health. “In a country with so much inequality and with a wide range of social problems, people don’t see science as a priority,” he says.

How philanthropy can nurture your research

But in 2017, one couple — documentarian João Moreira Salles and podcaster Branca Vianna — decided that Brazil needed a philanthropic organization devoted to basic research. The family founded the Serrapilheira Institute, which funds research by early-career scientists in the natural sciences, computer science and mathematics.

The organization has since become a case study for how it is possible to support science with philanthropy in Brazil despite regulatory hurdles and a tax system that doesn’t incentivize donations. Other initiatives in the country include Pioneer Science, an organization based in Rio de Janeiro that funds research in fields such as neuroscience and the physics and mathematics of biology, and the Pensi Institute in São Paulo, which supports research on child and adolescent health as well as in the social sciences and philanthropy.

Learning from mistakes

Now, some of those donors hope to bring more organizations into the fold. A handful of philanthropic institutions in Brazil, encouraged by philanthropy researchers at the University of São Paulo, are in the early stages of forming a local association inspired by the Science Philanthropy Alliance in the United States.

articles.title: One of the fundamental forces is stronger than we thought
articles.summary: The most precise calculation yet of the electroweak force could help fix cracks in the standard model of particle physics
articles.content:
The most precise calculation yet of the electroweak force could help fix cracks in the standard model of particle physics

Future particle colliders could use the new calculations Diego Grandi/Shutterstock

One of the universe’s fundamental forces appears to be stronger than we thought, a finding that could lead to the discovery of new particles.

The electroweak force unifies the electromagnetic and the weak nuclear forces. Under ordinary conditions, the two forces are distinct and play a role in different processes, such as the weak force being part of radioactive decay and the electromagnetic force affecting charged objects. But at very high energies and temperatures, like as seen in some stages of the early universe and in particle colliders, the two forces combine.

Alessandro Conigli at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany and his colleagues have now calculated several properties that capture the strength of the electroweak force with unprecedented precision and found a discrepancy with past calculations.

Advertisement

Calculating details of nuclear forces is notoriously difficult. For decades, researchers could only do so with “phenomenological methods” where they could not solve equations exactly but had to include inputs from experiments. This made it more difficult to say whether the best theoretical predictions agreed with experimental findings or not, as the two approaches were mixed.

In 2024, the phenomenological method was called into question when an experiment involving particles called muons appeared not to match theoretical calculations. However, when researchers refined these calculations using a new technique called lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD), everything worked again.

Conigli and his colleagues used this same technique to calculate two numbers that capture how quantum pairs of virtual particles and their antimatter “antiparticles” affect the strength of the electroweak force at different energy levels.

Across two studies, the team found that the lattice QCD results differed from the phenomenological calculations by around 1 per cent. While small, this discrepancy is significant because the researchers managed to halve the errors in their calculation. This level of precision is crucial for unravelling several mysteries that currently plague our understanding of particles.

Specifically, it will help in the search for phenomena not contained in the standard model of particle physics, which tabulates all known forces and particles, including the electroweak force. It is a remarkably well-tested theory of the world, yet it currently doesn’t explain important phenomena such as dark matter, which is very abundant in our universe.

The properties that the team calculated are badly needed to aid experimental searchers of new particles, says Colin Morningstar at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania. “I applaud the work very heartily,” he says.

Krishna Kumar at the University of Massachusetts Amherst says the biggest implications of the work will be for particle colliders that are yet to be built, such as the proposed Future Circular Collider, which will surpass the precision of existing experiments. “If you build a new collider, the question is, will you have the theoretical prowess you need to interpret the measurements?” says Kumar.

Conigli says that the new work ought to serve as an encouragement and a reason to keep building better and better colliders. “We truly believe that this could be a game changer,” he says.

Journal Reference: Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/r2cx-tl7s
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in precisely calculating the electroweak force, which could help resolve fundamental issues in the standard model of particle physics and guide future particle collider experiments. This advancement has broad implications for physics and our understanding of the universe, representing a meaningful and inspiring scientific progress.
articles.personality_title: New precise calculation shows electroweak force is stronger than expected
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
The electroweak force is one of the four fundamental forces in the universe. It combines the electromagnetic force, which affects charged particles, and the weak nuclear force, which causes radioactive decay. Scientists study this force to understand how particles behave and interact.

**What happened**
A team led by Alessandro Conigli at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz used a new method called lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD) to calculate the strength of the electroweak force more precisely than ever before. Their results showed the force is about 1% stronger than previous calculations suggested. This difference is small but important because their method reduces errors by half compared to older methods.

**Impact**
This improved calculation helps fix some problems in the standard model of particle physics, which is the main theory explaining particles and forces. The standard model doesn’t explain everything, like what dark matter is. The new findings could guide scientists in finding new particles that the standard model misses. It also means future experiments, especially with new particle colliders, will be better prepared to understand their results.

**What's next step**
Scientists plan to use these precise calculations to design and interpret experiments at future particle colliders, like the proposed Future Circular Collider. These machines will explore higher energies and may discover new particles or forces. The new calculations encourage building better colliders and help ensure scientists can understand what they find.

**One-sentence takeaway**
A more precise calculation reveals the electroweak force is stronger than thought, improving our understanding of particle physics and guiding future discoveries.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle mesure précise montre que la force électrofaible est plus forte que prévu
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
La force électrofaible est l’une des quatre forces fondamentales de l’univers. Elle combine la force électromagnétique, qui agit sur les particules chargées, et la force faible, responsable de la radioactivité. Les scientifiques l’étudient pour comprendre comment les particules interagissent.

**Ce qui s’est passé**
Une équipe dirigée par Alessandro Conigli à l’Université Johannes Gutenberg de Mayence a utilisé une nouvelle méthode appelée chromodynamique quantique sur réseau (QCD) pour calculer la force électrofaible avec une précision inégalée. Ils ont découvert que cette force est environ 1 % plus forte que ce que les calculs précédents indiquaient. Cette différence est petite mais importante car leur méthode réduit de moitié les erreurs par rapport aux anciennes techniques.

**Impact**
Cette meilleure mesure aide à résoudre certains problèmes du modèle standard de la physique des particules, qui explique la plupart des particules et forces connues. Ce modèle ne répond pas à toutes les questions, comme la nature de la matière noire. Ces résultats pourraient aider à trouver de nouvelles particules que le modèle standard ne prévoit pas. Ils préparent aussi mieux les expériences futures.

**Étape suivante**
Les scientifiques utiliseront ces calculs précis pour concevoir et interpréter les expériences dans de futurs accélérateurs de particules, comme le futur collisionneur circulaire proposé. Ces machines exploreront des énergies plus élevées et pourraient découvrir de nouvelles particules ou forces. Ces résultats encouragent à construire de meilleurs accélérateurs et à mieux comprendre leurs découvertes.

**En une phrase**
Une mesure plus précise montre que la force électrofaible est plus forte que prévu, améliorant notre compréhension de la physique des particules et guidant les futures découvertes.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo cálculo preciso muestra que la fuerza electrodébil es más fuerte de lo esperado
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
La fuerza electrodébil es una de las cuatro fuerzas fundamentales del universo. Combina la fuerza electromagnética, que afecta a las partículas cargadas, y la fuerza débil, que causa la desintegración radiactiva. Los científicos la estudian para entender cómo se comportan las partículas.

**Qué pasó**
Un equipo dirigido por Alessandro Conigli en la Universidad Johannes Gutenberg de Maguncia usó un método nuevo llamado cromodinámica cuántica en red (QCD) para calcular la fuerza electrodébil con una precisión nunca antes lograda. Descubrieron que la fuerza es aproximadamente un 1 % más fuerte que los cálculos anteriores. Esta diferencia es pequeña pero importante porque su método reduce el error a la mitad en comparación con técnicas antiguas.

**Impacto**
Este cálculo mejorado ayuda a corregir problemas en el modelo estándar de la física de partículas, que explica las partículas y fuerzas conocidas. El modelo estándar no explica todo, como la materia oscura. Este hallazgo puede ayudar a encontrar nuevas partículas que el modelo no incluye. También prepara mejor a los experimentos futuros.

**Próximo paso**
Los científicos usarán estos cálculos precisos para diseñar e interpretar experimentos en futuros colisionadores de partículas, como el propuesto Colisionador Circular Futuro. Estas máquinas explorarán energías más altas y podrían descubrir nuevas partículas o fuerzas. Este avance anima a construir mejores colisionadores y a entender mejor sus resultados.

articles.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
articles.summary: New rules introduced on Tuesday mean establishments will be able to accept digital ID apps alongside physical documents.
articles.content:
Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.
